knowledge-base.name: database
knowledge-base.triggers: database, SQL, schema, migration, query, index, ORM, PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, transaction, normalization, foreign key, JOIN, N+1, connection pool, EXPLAIN, deadlock, ACID
knowledge-base.overview: Database design, query optimization, and migration management for reliable data systems. Good database work prevents the hardest class of bugs: silent data corruption, irreversible state, and cascading performance failures.

form.name: 1NF
form.rule: Atomic columns — no repeating groups, no arrays in cells, one value per cell

form.name: 2NF
form.rule: No partial dependencies — every non-key column depends on the whole primary key, not part of it

form.name: 3NF
form.rule: No transitive dependencies — non-key columns depend only on the primary key, not on other non-key columns

form.name: BCNF
form.rule: Every determinant is a candidate key — stricter than 3NF, eliminates anomalies in tables with overlapping candidate keys

denormalization.when: Read performance is measurably critical and JOIN cost is proven by profiling
Reporting/analytics tables where write anomalies are acceptable
denormalization.require: Document reason in schema comments — denormalization without justification becomes technical debt

naming-conventions.rule: Primary keys: id (or table_id for clarity in JOINs)
Boolean columns: prefix with is_ or has_ (is_active, has_verified_email)
Timestamp columns: suffix with _at (created_at, updated_at, deleted_at)
Junction tables: both table names joined (user_roles, post_tags)

integrity-constraints.rule: Declare foreign key constraints — enforce referential integrity at the database level, not only in application code
Use NOT NULL for required columns — nullable columns require null-checks everywhere in code
Apply UNIQUE constraints where business rules demand uniqueness (email, slug)
Use CHECK constraints for column-level business rules (status IN ('active','inactive'), amount > 0)
Soft deletes: add deleted_at TIMESTAMP NULL and filter in queries — never rely on application-only deletion

index-types.type: Default. Supports equality, range, ORDER BY, and LIKE 'prefix%'. Use for most indexed columns.
Equality-only. Faster for = lookups but no range support. Rarely worth it over B-tree.
Index on multiple columns. Column order matters — put equality columns first, then range columns.
Index on a subset of rows (WHERE is_active = true). Smaller, faster for filtered queries.
Index includes all columns a query needs — eliminates table heap access entirely.
PostgreSQL full-text search, JSONB, array columns. Use only when needed.

when-to-index.index: Foreign key columns — always. Missing FK indexes cause full table scans on every JOIN or DELETE.
Columns in WHERE clauses of frequent queries
Columns in ORDER BY of paginated queries
Columns used in JOIN conditions that are not primary keys

when-not-to-index.avoid: Low-cardinality columns (boolean, status with 2-3 values) — planner may ignore the index anyway
Columns written far more than read — every index adds write overhead
Small tables — full scan is often faster than index lookup on <1000 rows
Indexing everything speculatively — prove with EXPLAIN before adding

composite-index-order.rule: ORDER BY columns last if they match the query sort direction
composite-index-order.example: Index on (status, created_at) serves: WHERE status = ? AND created_at > ? ORDER BY created_at

explain-plans.rule: Read EXPLAIN (or EXPLAIN ANALYZE in PostgreSQL) before declaring a query optimized
explain-plans.warning: EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query — use on non-destructive queries or in a transaction you roll back

red-flags.flag: Seq Scan on large table — missing index or index not being used
Nested Loop on large row counts — may need Hash Join or Merge Join
High row estimate error — stale table statistics; run ANALYZE
Sort without index — expensive for large result sets

join-optimization.rule: Index JOIN columns on both sides of the join
Filter as early as possible — narrow result sets before joining
Prefer explicit JOIN syntax over implicit comma-separated FROM
Avoid joining to subqueries that return large result sets; use CTEs or temp tables

subquery-vs-cte.cte: Use for readability and when the intermediate result is referenced more than once
subquery-vs-cte.subquery: Acceptable for simple one-off filters; avoid correlated subqueries on large tables
subquery-vs-cte.correlated-warning: Correlated subqueries execute once per row of the outer query — this is often the cause of unexpectedly slow queries

pagination.avoid: OFFSET for deep pagination — database still scans skipped rows
pagination.prefer: Keyset pagination: WHERE id > last_seen_id ORDER BY id LIMIT n

select-columns.rule: Never use SELECT * in production code — select only the columns needed
select-columns.reason: SELECT * fetches unused data across the wire, breaks when schema changes, prevents covering indexes

types.type: ALTER TABLE, CREATE INDEX, DROP COLUMN — changes database structure
Backfilling columns, transforming existing rows — changes database content
types.note: Keep schema and data migrations separate; data migrations on large tables can lock and block production traffic

reversibility.rule: Every migration must have a down/rollback path
Test rollback before deploying forward migration to production
reversibility.destructive: DROP COLUMN, DROP TABLE — add a deprecation period; rename first, remove in a later release

pattern.name: Expand-Contract
pattern.step: Expand: add new column (nullable), deploy code that writes both old and new
Backfill: populate new column for existing rows in batches
Switch: deploy code that reads from new column only
Contract: drop old column once traffic is fully migrated

zero-downtime.avoid: Adding NOT NULL column without a DEFAULT to a large table — locks the table during migration
Renaming columns in a single step — breaks running application instances

testing.rule: Run migrations against a clone of production data before applying to production
Time the migration on production-scale data — 100ms on dev can be 10 minutes on prod
Verify rollback works on the same clone
Confirm application still passes tests after migration + rollback cycle

acid.property: All writes in a transaction succeed or all are rolled back — no partial commits
Transaction brings database from one valid state to another — constraints enforced
Concurrent transactions don't see each other's partial state

isolation-levels.level: Sees uncommitted changes from other transactions. Almost never use.
Default in PostgreSQL/SQL Server. Only sees committed data. Prevents dirty reads.
Re-reading same row returns same result. Prevents non-repeatable reads. Default in MySQL InnoDB.
Full isolation — behaves as if transactions ran sequentially. Use for financial operations.

deadlock-prevention.rule: Always acquire locks in a consistent order across all transactions
Keep transactions short — commit or rollback as fast as possible
Avoid user interaction inside a transaction (never wait for HTTP response while holding a lock)
Use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE only when you will definitely update the row
Implement retry logic with exponential backoff for deadlock errors

strategy.name: Optimistic locking
strategy.description: No database lock held; use version column to detect conflict at commit time
strategy.when: Low contention, mostly-read data, long-running edits
strategy.code-example: UPDATE orders SET status = 'shipped', version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ?

strategy.name: Pessimistic locking
strategy.description: Hold a database lock for the duration of the operation
strategy.when: High contention, financial transactions, inventory decrement
strategy.code-example: SELECT * FROM inventory WHERE product_id = ? FOR UPDATE;

n-plus-one.description: Fetching a collection then issuing one query per item in a loop
n-plus-one.code-example: # BAD: 1 query for posts + N queries for each author posts = Post.query.all() for post in posts: print(post.author.name) # triggers a new query each iteration
# GOOD: eager load with JOIN in a single query posts = Post.query.options(joinedload(Post.author)).all() for post in posts: print(post.author.name) # no extra query

eager-vs-lazy.lazy: Default in most ORMs. Related data loaded on access. Causes N+1 if accessed in a loop.
eager-vs-lazy.eager: Loaded with JOIN in the initial query. Use when you know you need the relationship.
eager-vs-lazy.rule: Audit ORM-generated SQL in development — enable query logging and watch for repeated queries

raw-queries.when: Complex reporting queries, window functions, recursive CTEs, bulk operations
raw-queries.rule: Still use parameterized placeholders even in raw ORM queries — never concatenate user input
raw-queries.code-example: db.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = :email", {"email": email})

migration-generation.rule: Review ORM-generated migrations before applying — auto-generators miss partial indexes, custom constraints, and data migrations
Never blindly apply generated migrations to production without reading the SQL

pooling.rule: Always use a connection pool — opening a new connection per request is expensive (20-100ms overhead)
pooling.sizing: Start with: pool_size = (2 * number_of_cores) + 1. Adjust based on observed wait times.
pooling.rule: Set pool_timeout — fail fast rather than queue indefinitely when pool is exhausted
Set connection max_lifetime to recycle connections and avoid stale/dropped connections

timeouts.rule: Set query timeouts — unbounded queries can monopolize connections and degrade the whole pool
Set connection acquisition timeout — surface pool exhaustion as errors, not hangs
timeouts.code-example: engine = create_engine( DATABASE_URL, pool_size=10, max_overflow=20, pool_timeout=30, # seconds to wait for a connection from pool pool_recycle=1800, # recycle connections after 30 minutes )

retry-logic.rule: Retry transient connection errors with exponential backoff and jitter
Do not retry on constraint violations or business logic errors — only network/timeout failures
Cap retry attempts — unbounded retries can amplify database load during an outage

health-checks.rule: Implement a /health endpoint that verifies database connectivity
Use SELECT 1 as the health check query — minimal overhead
Alert on connection pool wait time spikes — early warning before pool exhaustion

parameterized-queries.rule: ALWAYS use parameterized queries or prepared statements — this is non-negotiable
parameterized-queries.code-example: # BAD: f-string in SQL cursor.execute(f"SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE user_id = {user_id}")
# GOOD: placeholder binding cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE user_id = %s", (user_id,))

encryption.at-rest: Enable database-level encryption at rest for databases containing PII or sensitive data

column-level.when: Particularly sensitive fields: SSN, credit card numbers, health data
column-level.rule: Encrypt at application layer before writing — database-level encryption does not protect against privileged DB access
Store encryption key separately from database (key management service)

passwords.rule: NEVER store passwords in plain text or with reversible encryption
Use Argon2id, bcrypt, or scrypt — not MD5, SHA-1, or plain SHA-256

audit-logging.rule: Log who changed what data and when for sensitive tables (users, payments, permissions)
Implement audit tables or use a CDC (Change Data Capture) pattern
Do not log sensitive column values (passwords, tokens, card numbers) in audit logs
audit-logging.code-example: CREATE TABLE audit_log ( id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, table_name TEXT NOT NULL, record_id BIGINT NOT NULL, action TEXT NOT NULL, -- INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE changed_by BIGINT, -- user_id changed_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(), old_values JSONB, new_values JSONB );

least-privilege.rule: Application database user should have only the permissions it needs — not superuser
Read replicas should use a read-only user
Migration scripts run with a separate elevated user, not the application user

strategies.strategy: Complete snapshot of the database. Simple to restore, expensive to store frequently.
Only changes since last backup. Faster, smaller; requires full + incremental chain to restore.
Continuous archiving of write-ahead log — enables point-in-time recovery (PITR).

point-in-time-recovery.rule: Enable WAL archiving or binary log (MySQL) so you can recover to any point, not just scheduled backup times
Test PITR procedure quarterly — a backup you haven't tested restoring is not a backup

testing-restores.rule: Regularly restore from backup to a staging environment and verify data integrity
Measure restore time — know your RTO (Recovery Time Objective) before you need it
Automate restore verification — don't rely on manual spot-checks

retention.rule: Keep daily backups for 30 days minimum; weekly for 1 year for regulated data
Store backups in a different region from primary database

slow-query-logs.rule: Enable slow query logging in all environments (not just production)
Set threshold at 100ms to catch problems early; tighten to 50ms for latency-sensitive services
slow-query-logs.tool: pg_stat_statements extension — aggregate query statistics without per-query logging overhead

index-usage-stats.tool: pg_stat_user_indexes — shows index scans vs heap scans; find unused indexes
index-usage-stats.rule: Remove unused indexes — they add write overhead with no read benefit
Check index bloat on high-write tables; REINDEX or pg_repack periodically

connection-pool-metrics.metric: Pool wait time — time spent waiting for a connection from the pool
Pool utilization — what percentage of connections are in use
connection-pool-metrics.rule: Alert when pool utilization exceeds 80% — scale pool or optimize query hold time

table-statistics.rule: Run ANALYZE (PostgreSQL) or ANALYZE TABLE (MySQL) after large data loads to update query planner statistics
Configure autovacuum (PostgreSQL) appropriately for high-write tables — bloat degrades performance silently

critical.item: No string concatenation in SQL — all queries parameterized
Multi-step writes wrapped in a transaction
Passwords hashed with Argon2id, bcrypt, or scrypt — never plain text
Migrations have a reversible down path

high-priority.item: No N+1 query patterns in ORM usage
EXPLAIN plan reviewed for new queries on large tables
Connection pool limits respected — no unbounded connection creation

suggestions.item: Audit logging on sensitive table mutations
Slow query logging enabled for new query paths
Migration tested on production-scale data clone
